title: The treasure and the pearl (Matthew 13:44–46)
hook: a man finds treasure in a field and, in joy, sells everything to buy it

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman lit a lamp and swept the whole house for one small coin, and when she found it she called the neighbors over. Your line was throw the party. Did you celebrate something you found again? Day twenty-seven.

A man is working a field that isn't his. Long day, hard ground. And his tool hits something that isn't a rock. He digs around it with his hands. It's a hoard, buried who knows how long ago, by who knows whom. He looks around. Nobody saw. So he covers it back up, walks home, and sells everything he owns. The house. The animals. The good coat. His neighbors think he's lost his mind. And he's grinning the whole time, because he knows what's in that field, and he buys it. Right next to that story, Jesus tells another: a merchant seeking fine pearls finds one of great price, and sells everything for it too. Two tiny stories. Today, the treasure and the pearl.
screen: `A TOOL HITS SOMETHING.` → `HE SELLS EVERYTHING.` → `A MERCHANT FINDS ONE PEARL.`

segments.voice: In Matthew each of these stories takes a verse or two. Notice that the two men arrive in opposite ways. The farmhand wasn't looking for anything; he stumbled on it. The merchant was out looking, seeking goodly pearls, as the King James puts it, and he found one. Christians hear both ways in the story: some people are found by faith on an ordinary afternoon, and some search for years. Now the line the whole story turns on. The old King James Bible says the man, having found the treasure, "for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath." For joy. Not because he was told to. Not as a sacrifice he grits his teeth through. He's not giving things up. He's trading up, and he knows it. That's the surprise hiding in here. Sell everything sounds like loss. The story hears a man who can't believe his luck. So what is the treasure? Jesus says the kingdom of heaven is like this. One reading goes like this: God's kingdom, God's life, is worth more than everything else you own, and finding it feels like joy. Another reading turns it the other way round. God is the one who gives everything, to buy back the field, or the one "pearl of great price" is each person, and the one who sells all to have it is Christ. Both readings are still preached. Here's a detail to take with you. The Greek word Matthew uses for treasure is thesauros: a store, a hoard, something laid up. Earlier in the same Gospel, Jesus says: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." So the treasure and the pearl ask one quiet question. What would make you that happy to let go?
screen: `ONE STUMBLES ON IT. ONE SEARCHES.` · `FOR JOY, NOT BECAUSE HE WAS TOLD.` · `NOT A LOSS. A TRADE UP.` · `WHO IS THE BUYER? TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `ONE PEARL OF GREAT PRICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you'd give everything for. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Don't reach for the right answer. Let it come up on its own. A person. A way of living. A kind of peace. If you pray, you can hold it in front of God and ask whether it's the treasure. If you don't, just hold it. Then notice how it feels to name it. Heavy, like duty? Or light, like the man walking home from the field? Stay with that feeling. The bell holds the time.
The treasure and the pearl. Two one-sentence stories about finding something so good that selling everything feels like winning.
screen: `THE TREASURE AND THE PEARL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in joy, not duty. Pick one thing you'll do today anyway, and do it the way the man walked home from the field: glad, not grim. Day twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians read these two parables as a picture of how much God's kingdom is worth, and some tell stories of people who left careers or comforts gladly to follow their faith. They're read in churches in the season when Matthew 13 comes around in the lectionary.

match.prompt: who's who in the two stories — tap the pairs.

the text says he sold it all "for joy thereof." he's trading up, and he knows it.
each of these parables takes only a verse or two in Matthew
Matthew 13:44 is the treasure, 13:45–46 the pearl. two tiny stories, side by side.
Christians all agree who the buyer is
one reading makes the buyer a person finding God's kingdom. another makes the buyer God, giving everything for us.

fork.setup: you're working someone else's field, and your tool hits a buried treasure. nobody saw. what do you do?
options: take it home tonight and say nothing.
cover it up, sell everything you own, and buy the field.
tell the owner and hope for a reward.
fork.reveal: he hides it again and, "for joy thereof," sells all he has and buys the field. the story doesn't stop to judge his ethics. it's about the joy.

original.note: Greek: treasure, a store of valuables. the word in Matthew 13:44, and in 6:21: where your treasure is.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about giving everything up.
what it means: a story about joy. he sells everything because he's found something worth more.
what a scholar hears: two readings, both still preached. the buyer is a person finding the kingdom, or the buyer is God, and the pearl of great price is us.

Hook adds color not in the text (working a field that isn't his, no banks, hoards buried in the ground, selling house and animals). Matthew 13:44 implies the field isn't his (he buys it); the rest is scene-setting. Confirm it reads as retelling, not scripture.

The 'other way round' reading (God/Christ as the buyer, the pearl as the church or the person) is attributed loosely to 'early teachers to modern ones'; confirm this is a fair description and whether a named teacher should be cited.
